title: Direct-cessation weaning of high-flow nasal cannula for infants with bronchiolitis on a general pediatric ward
subtitle: Evaluation design not yet settled: improvement cycles or a before-after comparison
statement: Infants with bronchiolitis spend a median of 52 hours on high-flow nasal cannula on the general pediatric ward, partly because weaning varies between attendings. A drafted protocol stops high flow directly after two stable hours in FiO2 of 40 percent or less. The team needs to know whether the protocol shortens time on high flow and length of stay without more re-escalation, PICU transfer or readmission, particularly in young infants, and how to evaluate it within one season.
whoAffected: Infants with bronchiolitis on high flow (about 110 a season), their parents, ward nurses and respiratory therapists who do the checks, and the PICU team that receives infants who deteriorate.
whatHurts: Unnecessary hours on high flow delay feeding, holding and discharge, and inconsistent weaning confuses families; stopping too early in a vulnerable infant could lead to re-escalation or PICU transfer.
currentPractice: Weaning is at each attending's discretion, stepwise or direct, with no shared criteria for a trial off or for restarting.
whyNow: The protocol has been drafted and signed off, the season starts in November, and families keep asking why weaning takes so long.
constraints: No research funding. The weaning protocol has to start with the winter season in November 2026. Two-hourly checks must fit existing nurse and respiratory therapist staffing, which is thinner at night. Evaluation data must come from the chart plus a short bedside log.
patientCenteredGoal: Infants come off high flow as soon as it is safe, go home sooner and are not harmed by stopping too early, and parents know the criteria for stopping and restarting.
summary: Problem framed; the evaluation design is left unresolved between improvement cycles and a before-after comparison until the evidence has been reviewed.
